findings.detail: The applicability text asserts that for every carry case (a+b >= 10) the product is 'a four-digit number where the 1 carries into the hundreds'. Exhaustive check over the 45 carry cases shows only 9 of them (n in {91..99}) actually produce a four-digit result; the other 36 produce three-digit numbers. The carry rule (a+1, a+b-10, b) is arithmetically correct, but the accompanying 'four-digit number' characterisation is false for 80% of the carry set (36/45). A student who reads the applicability line and computes 19*11 will get 209, not the promised four-digit answer.
findings.witness: n=19: digit sum 1+9=10 (carry case), 19*11 = 209 (three digits, not four).

findings.detail: Step s3 renders the carry as '9+1 | 1 | 2' and s4 states the result '1012'. The intermediate reasoning a viewer must perform — evaluate 9+1 = 10, place it in the hundreds column, observe that the 10 itself overflows so 1 spills into the thousands, yielding 1|0|1|2 — is not made explicit anywhere in the step sequence. The steps read in order do not literally produce '1012' without the reader silently filling in place-value overflow.
